segments.text: Hello, Hannah. Come and take a seat. What would you like to talk about today?
I'm not really sure where to start. I think I'm just anxious all the time and it's got worse in September.
What happened in September?
I was my deputy head at my school. I've taught here for 11 years and I love it.
And then the head asked me to step up when our deputy left.
That sounds like recognition of your work.
That's what everyone says, but I keep thinking they picked the wrong person and that sooner or later someone will notice I have no idea what I'm doing.
What does it look like when that thought arrives?
Mostly Sunday evenings. My chest goes tight and I start rehearsing Monday's stuff meeting in my head.
What do you rehearse?
Every possible question someone might ask and what I would say and what they would think of me if I got it wrong.
What do you imagine they would think?
That I'm out of my depth. That they gave the job to a nice ear for a teacher who can't actually lead.
Has anyone said anything that suggests that?
No, that's the strange thing. Nobody has. It's all in my head.
It's still very real to you?
Very. Last week I rewrote the same email to the governors four times.
Four times. What was the email about?
Change to the behavior policy. It was two paragraphs.
I was afraid Mr. Hargraves, the chair of governors, would think that I was stupid.
How does he treat you?
He has been nothing but kind. He told me in September he was delighted.
That makes it worse somehow. Because I feel like I'm lying to him.
Lying to him about what?
About being capable, as if I'm pretending.
Pretending to be what?
Somebody who knows what she's doing. Most days I feel like a child wearing her mother's coat.
That's a vivid image. Whose coat is that?
My mum's, I suppose. She was a head teacher for 20 years.
Tell me about that.
She was brilliant. Everyone in the village still stops me and say what a wonderful head she was.
She retired six years ago and they have named a library after her.
And you're now in a similar job?
A deputy's job. But yes. I can't help comparing.
Everything I do, I think, would she have done it better?
Does she say that?
Never. She's very supportive on the surface.
She says I've always worried too much and I should stop being silly.
How does it land when she says that?
It makes me feel like I'm making a fuss so I don't tell her how bad it is.
What does she not know?
That I'm awake at four every morning.
I fall asleep fine.
Then I'm awake at four going through the to-do list.
What else on the list?
Everything.
Timetable changes, the offset prep, a parent complaint, a child I'm worried about.
It goes round and round.
How long have you been waking like that?
Since about the second week of term.
I drink a lot of coffee to get through the day, which I know doesn't help.
How many cups?
Five or six.
Then I can't sit still in the afternoons.
What do you notice in your body during those afternoons?
My heart goes fast.
My hands are a bit shaky.
Last Thursday I had to leave a meeting to splash my face with water.
Did anyone notice?
I don't think so.
I said I was fetching a document.
That sounds like a lot of effort to hide it.
It is.
I'm exhausted by the end of every day.
Just from pretending.
Who knows how you're feeling?
My partner Ben knows a bit.
He says I should just enjoy it.
How do you feel when he says that?
Guilty and a bit alone.
He means well.
He's an engineer.
He thinks if something's a problem, you fix it.
You can't just fix this.
No.
I wish it were that simple.
Do you have friends at school?
You can talk to him.
Not anymore.
Not really.
I used to eat lunch in the year four quarter with the others.
Now I'm their line manager and it's awkward.
So you lost some company along with the promotion?
Yes.
I hadn't thought of it like that.
I miss them.
I miss my class too.
What do you miss most?
The children.
Mostly.
The daily bit where a child gets something for the first time.
Now my days are spreadsheets.
Do you want a day promotion?
I thought I did.
I said yes in the room because I couldn't say no to her.
The head.
Then I went home and cry.
What were the tears about?
A year I think.
And that I would never get to go back.
Would you want to go back?
I don't know.
That sounds terrible, doesn't it?
After everyone's been so supportive.
That sounds like an honest question.
Nobody has asked me, Dad.
They just say, well, Dan.
What was the last time you felt properly relaxed?
These summer holidays.
We went walking in the lakes.
And I didn't think about school once for ten days.
What was different, dear?
Nobody expected anything of me.
I was just walking.
Ben carried the sandwiches.
Yes.
Um, Dan.
The week before term, I was a wreck again.
I couldn't eat on the Sunday.
Is there anything you already tried to tell?
Even less than?
I started writing down what went well each evening.
Small things.
A chill laughing.
A good email.
How did that go?
It helped for about two weeks.
And then I stopped because I felt silly.
Silly in what way?
As if I were bragging to myself in a notebook.
Noticing what went well is not the same as bragging.
Probably not.
It just felt that way.
That sounds worth back coming, too.
Have you thought about whether there is something particular you'd like from our work?
I would like to do the job without feeling like a fraud.
What would that look like on a Tuesday?
Hmm.
Walking into a meeting and not rehearsing at first.
Sending an email once.
And on Sunday?
Being able to sit on the sofa in the evening without my stomach in knots.
Those are clear goals.
How do you feel now saying them out loud?
A light fall.
Lighter.
A bit tearful, actually.
That's alright.
Take a moment.
Sorry.
I didn't expect that.
There is nothing to apologize for.
What's coming up?
That's the first time I have told anyone how bad it is.
Not even Ben knows how about the 4 a.m.
What would it be like to tell him?
Scary.
It would probably be her that I didn't say sooner.
Would it be a reason to keep it to yourself?
I suppose...
No.
I might try this week.
What would help you do that?
If I choose a quiet moment, not on a Sunday evening, then I'm too warmed up.
Saturday morning, perhaps?
Yeah, over breakfast.
He's always in a good mood, Dan.
And one more small thing.
Would you try the evening notebook again, just for a week?
Even one line?
I could.
But I will put it by the kettle so I don't forget.
Alright, we're nearly out of time.
Is there anything you want to add?
One line that I nearly cancelled this morning.
I'm glad I didn't.
I'm glad too.
Same time next week.
Yes, please.
Thank you.
